worlds.name: Lab Meadow
worlds.tip: Why do SO₄²⁻ and “sulfate” belong together? They are the same ion, written as a formula and as a name. Flip the cards and match them!
worlds.blurb: Flip the cards to match names, formulae and shapes.

worlds.name: Orbital Ruins
worlds.tip: Try this: electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first (Aufbau), and spread out one by one before pairing up (Hund’s rule).
worlds.blurb: Push electrons into orbitals, following the rules that decide where each one goes.

worlds.name: Periodic Falls
worlds.tip: Did you know? The halogens are the elements in Group 17 of the periodic table.
worlds.blurb: Pop the element bubbles that match the sign, and build the periodic table as you go.

worlds.name: Trend Peaks
worlds.tip: Try this: ionisation energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
worlds.blurb: Hop up the mountain ledges in trend order: bigger atoms, easier electrons, stronger pulls. Down a group, then across a period.

worlds.name: Bond Glacier
worlds.tip: Try this: count the electron groups around the central atom. Lone pairs count too, and they change the shape.
worlds.blurb: Build Lewis structures by dragging bonds and lone pairs onto the ice, then name each molecule’s shape with VSEPR.

worlds.name: Ion Diner
worlds.tip: Why do ionic compounds have zero net charge? Because the total positive charge cancels the total negative charge. Serve a few customers and see!
worlds.blurb: Combine ions to serve ionic compounds before your customers lose patience.

worlds.name: Reaction Volcano
worlds.tip: Did you know? In a balanced equation every atom on the left turns up on the right. Atoms are rearranged, never made or destroyed.
worlds.blurb: Walk round the island, collect reactant molecules and mix them in the cauldron. The number you bring of each molecule is its coefficient.
